Open-source product blueprint · AGPL

Next-Gen
Download Platform

An original desktop download experience built on NSH, informed by Motrix 2.0's product architecture and MDM's Rust engine research — with a deliberate AGPL-3.0-or-later open-source strategy.

Original UXNSH + RustEngine-firstAGPL-3.0-or-laterDesktop + Headless
Important distinction
Motrix screenshots in this document are research references only. The proposed palette, visual direction, layouts, and interaction model are intentionally different. The technical plan distinguishes code reuse, architectural inspiration, and independent implementation.

01. Product North Star

Build a next-generation open-source download platform, not a Motrix clone. The product combines a reliable multi-protocol download service, a thoughtful desktop workspace, browser capture, automation interfaces, and optional headless/remote operation. Success means users trust it with large and important downloads, understand what the engine is doing, and can control complexity without being overwhelmed.

Product thesis
Reliability first. Intelligence second. Beauty throughout. Advanced power without advanced clutter.

02. Product Positioning & Differentiation

Position it as a powerful download workspace for people who regularly download large files, media, datasets, archives, torrents, and batches of links. Differentiate through transparent connection intelligence, reliable recovery, precise browser handoff, a refined task workspace, and a coherent desktop/server architecture. Avoid unsubstantiated claims such as “always faster than IDM” or “128 connections guarantees speed.”

03. Reference Product Research: What to Learn

Motrix 2.0: learn its separation of UI from the download core, shared desktop/headless core, MDXP JSON-RPC protocol, extension/native messaging integration, sandboxed plugin capabilities, dashboard customization, task activity charts, persistent sessions, and remote/server direction. MDM: study its independent Rust HTTP/FTP engine, dynamic segment planner, worker reuse, per-host limits, token-bucket speed limiting, atomic resume state, browser handoff rules, test lab with fault injection, and explicit architecture boundaries. NSH: use its native rendering and unstyled accessible primitives as a foundation, while owning the product's component library and visual language.

  • Motrix repository
  • MDM repository
  • NSH repository

04. Design Principles: Original, Not Motrix-Themed

Do not inherit Motrix's grey-green shell, black dashboard cards, purple-blue pixel glow, or exact page composition. Preserve only the underlying UX strengths: hierarchy, clarity, calmness, task visibility, and useful status. Create a distinct visual identity with its own palette, typography, spatial rhythm, icon system, empty-state illustrations, and interaction language. Design for real workflows before decoration.

05. Proposed Visual Direction: Quiet Precision

Recommended direction: Quiet Precision — a light, warm-neutral canvas paired with deep ink typography, restrained cobalt/teal action color, and a small set of semantic status colors. It should feel closer to a carefully crafted professional creative tool than a traditional download utility. Avoid generic SaaS gradients, excessive glass, over-rounded cards, neon, and black-on-black surfaces. Support a fully considered dark theme, but do not make dark mode the only identity.

07. Typography, Density & Geometry

Use platform system fonts by default, with an optional bundled family only if licensing and rendering quality justify it. Use tabular numerals for speed, size, ETA, peer counts, and percentages. Suggested desktop scale: page title 28–34px; section title 18–20px; task title 14–15px; body 13–14px; metadata 11–12px; key metric 32–44px. Establish three density modes: Comfortable, Standard, Compact. Use a 4px spacing base, 8/12/16/24/32 spacing steps, 10–14px control radii, and 16–22px large surface radii. Avoid making every surface a card.

08. Application Shell & Navigation

Use a restrained app shell with a compact collapsible sidebar and a flexible main workspace. Primary destinations: Overview, Downloads, Link Collector, Media, Torrents, Activity. Secondary destinations: Browser Integration, Plugins, Notifications, Settings. Do not expose every advanced capability in the primary navigation if it is rarely used; let task type and context reveal relevant controls. Support global Add Download, global search, command palette, and keyboard shortcuts.

09. Overview: A Useful Command Centre

Overview should answer: Is the engine healthy? What is downloading? Is bandwidth being used efficiently? What needs attention? Include a concise live throughput panel, active/queued/completed counts, recent activity, recent failures requiring action, and a compact engine/connection health summary. Make charts optional and meaningful; do not fill space with decorative heatmaps or meaningless lifetime totals. Let users customize or hide overview modules.

10. Downloads Workspace

Make the task list the primary work surface. Provide saved views: All, Active, Queued, Completed, Failed, Paused; allow user-defined filters. Each row should show filename, source host, task type, progress, current speed, ETA, status, and destination where useful. Use a clear progress visualization with optional segment detail on demand. Support multi-select, batch pause/resume/retry/remove, sorting, column configuration, grouping, search, context menus, drag-and-drop, and undo for destructive list operations. Keep the primary Add action visible.

11. Task Detail & Connection Inspector

Use a contextual detail drawer or split inspector, not a permanent full-width detail page. Overview: file identity, source, total size, downloaded bytes, hash/checksum when available, destination, timestamps, and status. Connections: active workers, remote endpoints, per-connection throughput, retry count, and host limits. Segments: segment map and state transitions. Request: protocol, redirects, selected headers, validators, range support. Logs: concise event timeline with export. Redact cookies, authorization headers, and signed query parameters by default.

12. Add Download Flow

Support paste URL, drag/drop URL or torrent file, browser-captured downloads, magnet links, batch URL import, and clipboard detection with user permission. Before starting, show filename, destination, category, connection policy, and any required credentials. Progressive disclosure: ordinary users see a clean confirmation; advanced users can expand headers, proxy, checksum, connection cap, scheduling, and per-task speed limit. Detect duplicate tasks and existing files with explicit choices.

13. Link Collector & Batch Operations

Create a dedicated collection workflow for multiple links. Parse pasted text, page-captured links, supported link lists, and browser context. Show detected file names, types, sizes when known, hosts, and package grouping. Allow include/exclude rules, rename templates, destination rules, and queue assignment. Make extraction and debrid providers optional integrations with explicit permissions and clear account-secret handling.

14. Media & Gallery Downloads

Treat media acquisition as a task family, not an invisible side effect of generic HTTP. Integrate yt-dlp and gallery-dl as external tools where appropriate, with version detection, update strategy, process supervision, cancellation, and structured output parsing. Provide format/quality selection, audio-only, subtitles, playlist selection, and gallery item selection. Respect source-site terms and user rights; do not imply DRM circumvention. Keep external tool logs available for diagnosis.

15. Torrent Workspace

Use a dedicated Torrent task detail model. Show torrent metadata, selected files, trackers, peers, seeders/leechers, piece progress, download/upload rates, ratio, and seeding policy. Support magnet and .torrent inputs, sequential download where supported, per-torrent limits, queueing, and tracker editing. Keep BitTorrent-specific concepts out of ordinary HTTP task rows. Evaluate librqbit integration and compatibility before committing to feature parity claims.

16. Engine Strategy: Reuse First, Improve Deliberately

Do not concatenate Motrix and MDM codebases. Use Motrix as an architectural/product reference and MDM as the primary engine implementation reference. First assess whether mdm-engine can be consumed as a library under its GPL-3.0-or-later terms, then isolate it behind a stable internal engine interface. If direct reuse is not practical, implement independently from protocol specifications and documented behavior, using clean-room boundaries. Keep a replaceable engine adapter so the UI and task model are not coupled to one implementation.

17. MDM Engine: What to Study or Reuse

MDM's documented HTTP(S)/FTP(S) engine includes probing, validators (ETag/Last-Modified), a pure segment planner, worker connections reused across segments, dynamic splitting of remaining work, dropping slow workers and re-splitting their ranges, per-host connection limits, shared token-bucket limiters, and atomically persisted resume state. Study its tests and fault-injection lab, not just its README claims. Verify current crate APIs, internal visibility, feature flags, platform support, and library suitability before deciding to depend on it. Its Torrent functionality is a separate librqbit-backed crate; media/gallery tools are external programs.

18. Engine Improvements: A Measurable Backlog

Potential improvements to investigate: adaptive connection caps based on server behavior; smarter segment sizing informed by throughput and RTT; fairness between tasks; per-host congestion awareness; robust handling of servers that ignore Range; validator changes during resume; redirect and expiring URL refresh; bounded retry with classified errors; atomic state snapshots; disk-space preflight; checksum verification; per-network-interface binding; proxy/DNS policies; and detailed diagnostics. Each improvement must be backed by a test and benchmark. Do not assume HTTP/3 or more connections automatically improve segmented downloads.

19. Protocol & Capability Matrix

HTTP/HTTPS: range requests, redirects, cookies/headers, resume validators, proxy, authentication, checksums. FTP/FTPS: support only where tested and required. BitTorrent: separate engine adapter with magnet, torrent metadata, peer and piece state. Media: external extractor orchestration with structured task state. Archives: optional extraction workers. Debrid: optional provider adapters. Keep capability declarations explicit so the UI never offers an unsupported action.

20. Unified Task Domain Model

Define a common Task envelope: id, kind, source, display_name, destination, status, created_at, updated_at, progress, speed, eta, priority, labels, error, and engine_id. Use typed task-specific payloads: HttpTask, FtpTask, TorrentTask, MediaTask, ArchiveTask. Model lifecycle transitions explicitly; distinguish queued, probing, downloading, verifying, completed, paused, retrying, failed, cancelled, and seeding. Avoid a single giant struct full of optional fields.

21. Platform Architecture: Desktop, Service, CLI

Recommended layers: domain (task models and lifecycle); engine-api (traits/events); engine-mdm adapter or independent engine; torrent adapter; media tool adapter; scheduler; storage; browser host; protocol/API; telemetry/diagnostics; desktop shell; headless service; CLI; MCP integration. Desktop UI must not own download state. Headless service and desktop should use the same application services and task store. Separate OS integrations behind platform adapters.

22. NSH Implementation Strategy

NSH is a UI framework, not a ready-made product design system. Build the product's own component library on NSH primitives and unstyled base components. Verify the current native backend behavior, window chrome, table/list virtualization options, file dialogs, drag-and-drop, notifications, tray/menu integration, accessibility, and packaging on macOS/Windows/Linux. Prototype the highest-risk UI surfaces before committing. Use Rust for core services and high-frequency state; use TSX for screens where iteration speed is valuable. Avoid assuming browser CSS behavior or a prebuilt styled component kit.

23. IPC, Events & Update Frequency

Use typed commands for add, pause, resume, cancel, retry, reorder, configure, and query. Use events for task lifecycle, progress samples, connection changes, errors, and engine health. Coalesce progress updates and publish at a bounded UI cadence; do not emit one UI event per network chunk. Keep detailed segment telemetry available on demand. Version the local API and define authentication/authorization for remote access. Consider MDXP as a protocol reference, not a requirement to clone it.

24. Persistence, Recovery & File Safety

Use SQLite for task metadata, settings, queues, and event summaries; use engine-native atomic state files where appropriate. Define crash recovery, interrupted writes, partial file naming, validator checks, final size/hash verification, destination collisions, disk-full behavior, and cleanup. Never claim resume safety until crash/restart and server-change tests pass. Keep secrets in OS keychain/credential storage; store references, not plaintext credentials, in normal settings.

25. Browser Integration & Native Messaging

Build browser extensions for Chromium and Firefox where feasible, plus a native messaging host. The extension should hand off a download only after the desktop/service confirms acceptance; otherwise the browser should continue its normal download. Capture only the metadata needed for the task, such as URL, referrer, and user-authorized cookies. Provide per-site rules, file-type filters, exclusions, pause/resume handback behavior, and transparent permission explanations. Protect secrets in IPC and logs.

26. Plugin System & Capability Security

Separate trusted built-in integrations from third-party plugins. Define a versioned manifest, permissions, entry point, compatibility range, signature/source policy, and lifecycle. Capabilities should be narrow: resolve URL, transform filename, add metadata, provide a destination rule, or add a provider integration. Plugins must not receive arbitrary filesystem, process, network, or secret access by default. Run untrusted plugin code in a sandbox with explicit grants and resource limits.

27. Headless, Remote, CLI & MCP

Plan a shared service layer so the same task engine can run with a desktop UI or headless on NAS/server. Provide CLI commands for scripting and an authenticated local API. Remote control should require pairing and scoped tokens, TLS for network exposure, origin/host checks, and rate limits. An MCP server can expose safe task operations to AI tools, with destructive operations requiring confirmation. Treat remote control as a later milestone, not an MVP blocker.

28. AGPL-3.0-or-later Licensing Policy

Set the repository's project license to GNU AGPL-3.0-or-later, with SPDX identifiers in source headers where appropriate and a complete THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES/DEPENDENCIES inventory. MDM is GPL-3.0-or-later; AGPLv3 Section 13 provides a compatibility path for combining a covered GPLv3 work with an AGPLv3 work, but reuse still requires preserving notices, source obligations, and license conditions. Confirm the exact license files of every crate and bundled tool. Motrix's MIT code and NSH's Apache-2.0 code can generally be used under their terms, while preserving notices and checking dependency-specific conditions. AGPL network-use obligations apply to modified covered versions made available for remote network interaction. Do not describe AGPL as prohibiting commercial use; it does not. Obtain legal review for distribution and plugin boundary questions.

License gate
Before copying MDM code, verify the exact license text and dependency notices in the checked-out commit, decide whether the project will be AGPL-3.0-only or AGPL-3.0-or-later, and document the combination rationale. This plan assumes AGPL-3.0-or-later. This is engineering guidance, not legal advice. VideoDown's current main-branch README states that its current first-party code is under PolyForm Strict License 1.0.0 (non-commercial), while older releases previously published under GPLv3 remain under the license applicable to those releases. Therefore, do not copy current-main VideoDown code into this AGPL project. Study its workflow and architecture; reuse code only from a specifically identified historical GPLv3 commit/tag after checking its exact files and third-party notices.

29. Roadmap & Milestones

M1 Foundation: task domain, storage, engine adapter, HTTP download, recovery, basic browserless add flow. M2 Desktop MVP: original design system, Overview, Downloads, Inspector, settings, notifications, packaging. M3 Reliability: benchmark harness, fault injection, per-host policy, advanced resume and diagnostics. M4 Browser capture and Link Collector. M5 Torrent and Media integrations. M6 Headless service, CLI, remote pairing, MCP, plugin ecosystem. Release only when each milestone passes explicit acceptance criteria.

30. Benchmark & Performance Methodology

Compare against current Motrix, MDM, aria2, and IDM where available and legally testable. Use identical files, servers, network conditions, machine, OS, and default configuration. Include single-connection and multiple-connection scenarios; low/high RTT; packet loss; servers with and without Range; concurrent tasks; rate limits; expired URLs; interrupted transfers; restart recovery; and large files. Record median and P95 completion time, throughput, CPU, RAM, disk I/O, connection count, retries, and hash correctness. Publish raw data and harness. Never convert a single best-case result into a universal “X times faster” claim.

ScenarioMatrixMetrics
Connections1 / 4 / 8 / 16 / 32 / 64Throughput, finish time, CPU
NetworkRTT, packet loss, disconnectRetry count, recovery, failure rate
Server behaviorRange/no Range, 403, redirects, expiryFallback correctness, completion
Concurrency1 / 10 / 50 / 100 tasksTotal throughput, RAM, UI latency
IntegrityRestart, resume, file mutationHash match, corrupt output rate

31. Test Strategy & Release Gates

Unit-test planner and state transitions; property-test segment boundaries; integration-test against a local fault-injection server; end-to-end test browser handoff and recovery; verify torrent/media adapters independently. Test Windows/macOS/Linux packaging, signing, permissions, keychain, path edge cases, long filenames, Unicode, sleep/wake, proxy, VPN interface changes, and disk-full behavior. UI gates: keyboard navigation, focus, screen reader labels, contrast, reduced motion, small-window behavior, large task lists, and no misleading mock status.

32. Recommended MVP Scope

MVP should be narrow but excellent: HTTP/HTTPS downloads, reliable probe and resume, adaptive segmented downloading with safe fallback, queue and global/per-task limits, SQLite task history, clean add flow, downloads workspace, task inspector, Overview with live metrics, native notifications, and a browser extension only after core handoff semantics are stable. Defer BitTorrent, video extraction, debrid, plugin marketplace, remote server, and MCP until the HTTP foundation is trustworthy.

33. Coding Agent Rules & Repository Governance

Before implementation, read NSH's current Coding Guides and Design Guides, MDM's architecture and license files, and Motrix's current architecture docs. Never invent framework APIs. Produce an architecture decision record before choosing engine reuse. Build tokens and primitives before pages. Every UI feature needs loading/empty/error/populated states. Mock data must be visibly marked. Each vertical slice must include tests, screenshots, benchmark notes where relevant, and a license/dependency update. Keep AGPL headers and third-party notices correct.

34. Definition of Done

A release candidate must: download and resume correctly under injected failures; preserve file integrity; expose truthful engine status; avoid leaking secrets; behave correctly when the browser app is unavailable; handle large task lists without UI stalls; support keyboard and accessibility basics; build on supported target platforms; include source and dependency notices; and publish reproducible benchmark results for performance claims.

35. Platform Video Downloads: VideoDown-Class Workflow

Add a dedicated Video Downloads workspace for creator platforms and supported media URLs. The workflow is more than pasting a URL: authenticate where required; browse creators, uploads, favorites, collections, playlists, and multi-part videos; resolve available formats; choose resolution, codec, frame rate, HDR where exposed, audio track, subtitles, and audio-only output; enqueue one item or a batch; preserve source grouping and download history. Initial provider targets: YouTube, Bilibili, and Douyin, subject to platform terms, regional availability, and ongoing API maintenance. Provider support must be modular because platform APIs, signatures, cookies, and anti-abuse behavior change.

36. Video Provider Architecture

Define a VideoProvider interface with capabilities such as resolve_url, authenticate, refresh_session, list_creator_items, list_playlist_items, list_collections, get_formats, get_subtitles, and create_download_plan. Each provider returns normalized MediaItem and FormatOption models; it does not own the global queue or UI. Isolate provider-specific API clients and parsers. Support public URL mode and optional user-authorized account mode. Store cookies and tokens in OS secure storage, never in logs or plain exported settings. Add contract tests with sanitized fixtures and provider schema versions.

37. Video Download Pipeline: Resolve → Select → Fetch → Remux

Model the pipeline as explicit stages: URL intake; metadata resolution; format selection; stream planning; audio/video fetch; remux or merge; metadata/subtitle attachment; integrity validation; final atomic move; history indexing. Some platforms expose a single progressive file; others expose separate video and audio streams. Use FFmpeg as an optional external media tool for merging/remuxing and supported post-processing, with binary discovery, version checks, cancellation, progress parsing, and clear missing-tool guidance. Prefer stream copy/remux where possible; do not re-encode unless explicitly requested. Support subtitle language selection, embedded/external subtitle handling, thumbnail and metadata sidecars, naming templates, and per-provider output rules.

38. Video UX: Discovery, Format Picker & Batch Queue

The Video Downloads area has three connected views: Discover (provider browsing and pasted URL resolution), Selection (format/quality/audio/subtitle options), and Queue (download and merge state). Show title, creator, duration, thumbnail, source platform, and playlist context. Present formats in plain language: Best available, 1080p, 720p, audio only; an advanced expander reveals codec, container, bitrate, frame rate, HDR, and file size. For playlists/collections, select individual items, ranges, all loaded items, or filter by title/date/duration. Batch actions preserve grouping while allowing per-item overrides. Distinguish queued, resolving, downloading video, downloading audio, merging, verifying, and completed.

39. Torrent Video: Playback While Downloading

Treat “边下边播” as a first-class feature built on the torrent engine, not as a generic download option. User adds a magnet or .torrent, inspects metadata, selects a video file, and chooses Play While Downloading. The engine creates a playback session and prioritizes pieces required near the playback cursor, then maintains a forward buffer while downloading remaining pieces in the background. It must prioritize metadata and required container/index regions, handle padding files and multi-file torrents, and expose a minimum-buffer/readiness state before launching playback. Dandanplay documents playback before completion and launching this mode from an existing BT task; use that as a workflow reference, not as code to copy.

Core behavior
Select a video inside a torrent → buffer enough to start → play immediately → seek and reprioritize pieces → finish downloading in the background → continue or stop seeding according to user policy.

40. Playback-Aware Piece Scheduler & Local Stream Bridge

Add a PlaybackCoordinator above the BitTorrent engine. It receives playback position, seek requests, playback rate, and buffer health from the player; translates them into piece-priority windows; and informs the torrent engine without bypassing peer/request limits. Priorities: (1) pieces needed for the current seek target, (2) configurable forward buffer, (3) smaller safety window behind the playhead, (4) remaining pieces by normal swarm strategy. On seek, reprioritize quickly and cancel obsolete low-priority requests where permitted. Provide a loopback-only HTTP Range server or native stream bridge that serves verified/available byte ranges and waits within bounded timeouts. Keep temporary storage compatible with piece verification. On completion, transition seamlessly to ordinary seeding policy. Expose buffer seconds, playable range, current piece window, peer availability, and stall reason.

Player position / seek / playback rate
              ↓
       PlaybackCoordinator
              ↓
  Piece priority windows + buffer policy
              ↓
       BitTorrent engine
              ↓
    Verified piece storage
              ↓
 Loopback HTTP Range / native stream bridge
              ↓
        mpv / external player

41. Integrated Player & Media Compatibility

Use a proven playback engine rather than writing a codec stack. Evaluate libmpv/mpv and other cross-platform options against NSH embedding, hardware decoding, subtitle rendering, HDR, audio passthrough, accessibility, and packaging. Support external-player handoff as an initial fallback. The player understands the local stream bridge, seek feedback, pause/resume, audio/subtitle selection, playback speed, and graceful end-of-stream while the torrent is still completing. Display a clear distinction between playable/buffered, downloaded, and verified. Closing the player must not cancel the torrent; the download must continue safely.

42. Xunlei-Like Acceleration: What Is Realistic

Separate standard BitTorrent swarm optimization from proprietary P2SP/cloud acceleration. Implement legitimate multi-source acquisition where the user supplies authorized HTTP mirrors or direct source URLs, verify chunks against trusted hashes, and coordinate them with the torrent piece map. Also consider peer discovery, tracker health, DHT/PEX, IPv6, NAT traversal where supported, and LAN peer discovery. Xunlei's private cloud acceleration network, account entitlements, and proprietary server infrastructure are not an open protocol that can simply be cloned. Do not promise Xunlei-equivalent speed or access. Design a SourceProvider interface for user-configured mirrors, LAN peers, and future lawful providers; require integrity checks before accepting data from non-swarm sources.

CapabilityPlanBoundary
BT swarm optimizationImplement / tuneStandard protocol
User-provided HTTP mirrorsHash-verified supportUser must have access
LAN peer sharingPotential later featureOpt-in, trusted network
Xunlei private cloud nodesNo compatibility claimProprietary service/API

43. Video, Torrent & Account Safety

Treat provider cookies, authorization tokens, signed media URLs, and torrent metadata as sensitive. Redact secrets from diagnostics and crash reports. Require explicit confirmation before using account credentials or capturing browser cookies. Do not bypass DRM, paywalls, access controls, or platform restrictions; support content the user is authorized to access and comply with provider terms and local copyright law. For torrent streaming, show the torrent file list, total size, selected files, and seeding behavior before starting. Offer stop seeding, seed for a ratio/time, or continue seeding, explaining that BitTorrent may upload pieces during playback. Provide per-task and global upload caps.

44. Expanded Roadmap: Video & Torrent Streaming

MVP-A: HTTP/HTTPS reliability and task workspace. M2: video provider foundation plus one provider, URL resolution, format picker, audio/video merge, subtitles, and batch queue. M3: expand providers to YouTube/Bilibili/Douyin only as adapters pass compliance and regression tests. M4: torrent engine adapter, magnet/.torrent, file selection, metadata/peer/trackers, standard download and seeding. M5: playback bridge and playback-aware piece scheduling, first with a supported external player, then integrated player if platform embedding is viable. M6: source-provider framework for authorized mirrors/LAN peers, remote media library, subtitle/media metadata enrichment. Keep Xunlei-style private cloud acceleration out of committed milestones unless a lawful, documented provider API becomes available.
